goals: Explain the difference between logistics and supply chain management.
Describe the flows in a supply chain: products, information, money and returns.
Map a supply chain using the five stages of the SCOR model.
Use the Six Rights to check whether a supply chain decision is good.
Use FLOW and the Frame–Evaluate–Act–Review method to think through a decision.
Describe what makes a supply chain digital.

handout.intro: A supply chain is every step a product takes to reach the customer. This session gives you the words and tools we will use for the whole course.

blocks.p: Think about a carton of fresh milk in a Doha supermarket. Before it reaches the shelf, it passes through many hands: a dairy farm, a factory that pasteurises and packs it, a cold store, a refrigerated truck and finally the store.
All of these organisations, and all the steps between them, form one **supply chain**. Each step depends on the one before it.

callout.title: Upstream and downstream
callout.text: **Upstream** means towards the suppliers (the farm). **Downstream** means towards the customer (the shopper).

sections.h: 2. Logistics and supply chain management are not the same

head: Logistics
Supply chain management (SCM)
rows: The whole network, from raw materials to the customer
How do we transport, store, pick and deliver?
Who are our suppliers? How much do we make? How do all parts work together?
Booking a refrigerated truck for the milk
Agreeing a weekly plan with the farm, the factory and the stores

blocks.p: A simple way to remember it: **the supply chain is the whole system; logistics is the engine that moves it.**

list: **Products** flow downstream: from supplier to customer.
**Information** flows both ways: orders, forecasts, tracking updates and delivery confirmations.
**Money** flows upstream: the customer pays the store, the store pays the supplier.
**Returns** flow backwards: damaged items, recycling and repairs. This is called **reverse logistics**.

callout.title: Why information matters
callout.text: A shipment can arrive on time but still be stopped at customs because a document is wrong. When information fails, the products stop too.

blocks.p: The **SCOR model** (Supply Chain Operations Reference) is used around the world to describe any supply chain in the same way. We use its five classic stages, and each stage has its own colour on this site.

callout.title: Good to know
callout.text: In 2022 the Association for Supply Chain Management (ASCM) updated the model. The new version, SCOR DS, uses seven processes: Orchestrate, Plan, Order, Source, Transform, Fulfil and Return. Make became Transform, and Deliver was split into Order and Fulfil. The idea is the same.

blocks.p: A good supply chain gets six things right. Use them as a checklist for any decision or problem.

head: Right
Question to ask
rows: Is it exactly what the customer ordered?
Is it where it is needed?
Does it arrive when it is needed, not too late and not too early?
Is the cost right for the service the customer needs? (Not always the lowest cost.)
Do people have accurate, up-to-date information?
Was it the best choice with the information available?

blocks.p: When something goes wrong, ask: **which right was broken?** A late delivery is a time failure. A wrong item is a product failure. A decision made from old stock records is an information failure, and it usually causes a decision failure too.

sections.h: 6. Trade-offs: you cannot improve one part alone

blocks.p: Every part of the supply chain affects the others. Improving one part can make another part worse.

list: Holding less stock saves warehouse cost, but may need more frequent deliveries, so transport costs rise.
Choosing the cheapest supplier saves money today, but poor quality can increase returns tomorrow.
Air freight is fast, but it can cost many times more than sea freight.

blocks.p: A Level 6 professional looks at the **whole chain**, not only their own department.

sections.h: 7. FLOW: four disciplines for the whole course

head: Letter
Meaning
In practice
rows: Predict demand, risks and capacity before they happen.
Share information with suppliers, warehouses, transport and customers.
Find better ways without hurting quality or service. Not just cutting cost.
Measurable results: on time, in full, at the right cost, every time.

sections.h: 8. How to make a decision: Frame, Evaluate, Act, Review

steps: **Frame** – Define the real problem and the limits (time, money, space, information).
**Evaluate** – List the options and compare them with data, not opinion. Ask what could go wrong.
**Act** – Carry out the choice and tell everyone affected.
**Review** – Compare the result with what you expected. What will you do differently next time?

callout.title: Example
callout.text: Customers complain about late deliveries. Framing it as a transport problem is easy, but the real cause may be slow picking in the warehouse. A good frame saves time and money.

blocks.p: A **digital supply chain** captures every event as data and shares it in one place, so everyone works from **one version of the truth**.

head: Tool
What it records
rows: Which item was received, picked or shipped (scanned one by one)
Many items at once, without scanning each one
Where a truck or container is right now
Conditions such as temperature or shock during transport
Orders, stock, money and warehouse movements in one system

blocks.p: Data is only useful when it reaches the right person in time. A temperature alert from a milk truck matters only if the warehouse sees it **before** the milk goes on the shelf.

terms.meaning: All the organisations and steps that bring a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.example: Farm → factory → cold store → truck → supermarket.

terms.meaning: Planning and carrying out the movement and storage of goods and information.
terms.example: Booking a truck and storing pallets in a warehouse.

terms.meaning: Managing the whole network so that all parts work together.
terms.example: Agreeing one weekly plan with suppliers, factory and stores.

terms.meaning: Towards the suppliers and raw materials.
terms.example: The dairy farm is upstream of the supermarket.
The supermarket is downstream of the factory.

terms.meaning: Moving goods backwards in the chain for return, repair, reuse or recycling.
A standard model that describes any supply chain in five stages: Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return.
terms.example: Mapping a company's activities onto the five stages.

terms.meaning: Right product, place, time, cost, information and decision: a checklist for supply chain performance.
terms.example: A late delivery breaks the 'right time'.

terms.meaning: Giving up some of one thing to get more of another.
terms.example: Faster air freight, but a higher cost.

terms.meaning: Forecast, Link, Optimize, Win: four disciplines of a well-run supply chain.
terms.example: Sharing the forecast with suppliers is 'Link'.

terms.meaning: The time between placing an order and receiving it.
terms.example: The supplier delivers 5 days after the order.

terms.meaning: Being able to see where goods, orders and stock are at any time.
terms.example: Tracking a container on a map.

terms.meaning: A supply chain that captures events as data and shares it in one system.
terms.example: Barcode scans update stock levels immediately.

terms.meaning: Everyone uses the same, up-to-date data instead of separate spreadsheets.
terms.example: Sales and the warehouse see the same stock figure.

quiz.q: Which sentence best describes the difference between logistics and supply chain management?
options: They mean exactly the same thing.
Logistics moves and stores goods; supply chain management manages the whole network.
Logistics is only about money; supply chain management is only about trucks.
Supply chain management is a small part of logistics.
quiz.why: The supply chain is the whole system. Logistics is the engine that moves and stores the goods inside it.

quiz.q: A dairy farm supplies a factory that supplies a supermarket. From the supermarket's point of view, the farm is…
quiz.why: Upstream means towards the suppliers and raw materials.

quiz.q: Which flow usually moves upstream, from the customer towards the supplier?
quiz.why: The customer pays the store, and the store pays its supplier, so money moves upstream.

quiz.q: A customer returns a damaged phone so it can be repaired. This is part of…
quiz.why: Reverse logistics moves goods backwards for return, repair, reuse or recycling.

quiz.q: In the SCOR model, choosing and buying from suppliers belongs to which stage?
quiz.why: Source covers buying materials and services from suppliers.

quiz.q: An order arrives on time and in the right place, but it contains the wrong item. Which of the Six Rights was broken?
quiz.why: The wrong item is a product failure.

options: The cost that gives the required service without waste
The highest cost, for the best quality
The cost the supplier asks for
quiz.why: The right cost is not always the lowest. It is the cost that delivers the service the customer needs, without waste.

quiz.q: A warehouse cuts its stock to save money. Now the trucks must deliver twice as often. This is an example of…
quiz.why: Saving in one area (stock) created a cost in another (transport). That is a trade-off.

quiz.q: In FLOW, sharing your forecast with your suppliers so they can plan is an example of…
quiz.why: Link means connecting the parts of the chain with shared information.

quiz.q: Which tool can read many items at once, without scanning each one?
quiz.why: RFID tags are read by radio, so many items can be counted at once without line-of-sight.
